records.title: A Local Law in relation to requiring the commissioner of health and mental hygiene to establish and operate a pilot program providing free mental health services to children who have been returned to their home following a removal, and providing for the repeal of such provisions upon the expiration thereof
agencies_full: Department of Health and Mental Hygiene

program_breakdowns.program: Mental Health Services Pilot Program - Social Workers
program_breakdowns.description: Hiring of two social workers to administer mental health services to reunified children for the three-year pilot program.
program_breakdowns.offset_notes: Total includes prorated costs: $159,688 (FY27), $217,485 (FY28), $217,485 (FY29), $57,797 (FY30)

records.impact_narrative_revenue: It is anticipated that there would be no impact on revenues as a result of this legislation.
records.impact_narrative_expenditure: The Council estimates that total cost of the enactment of this legislation would be $652,455 to hire two social workers to fulfill this legislation's requirements for the three-year period of the pilot. The annual salary for each social worker is estimated to be $72,495 with a 50 percent fringe rate for a total cost of $108,743 per year for each position. Because this legislation is anticipated to be effective for only a portion of Fiscal 2027, the prorated costs in that year are estimated to be $159,688. For Fiscals 2028 and 2029, the cost is estimated to be $217,485 per year. In Fiscal 2030 the cost is estimated to be $57,797, which is prorated for the portion of the year the program would be effective before it is deemed repealed. The Council estimates the pilot program would operate with 50 slots for eligible families and the two social workers to administer services. Based on the Council's analysis of current ACS operations and understanding of the removal process, youth who have been removed from their families and then reunified are typically already participating in court-mandated or other ACS-provided mental health services as part of the reunification process and the demand for this program is likely to only require the hiring of two additional social workers for the duration of the pilot.
records.omb_estimate_notes: The Office of Management and Budget did not provide an estimate.

records.title: A Local Law to amend the administrative code of the city of New York, in relation to requiring all schools to stock airway clearance devices, and to repeal section two of such local law upon the expiration thereof

program_breakdowns.description: One-time purchase of airway clearance devices (one case per school) for 2,734 schools citywide.

records.impact_narrative_revenue: It is estimated that there would be no impact on revenues resulting from the enactment of this legislation. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB)'s estimate of this legislation's impact on the City's revenues is consistent with the Council's estimate.
records.impact_narrative_expenditure: It is estimated that there would be an impact on expenditures resulting from the enactment of this legislation. The Department of Education (DOE) would need to provide airway clearance devices to 2,734 schools, including public, charter and private schools as of the 2024-2025 school year. Airway clearance devices would be defined by the proposed legislation as a medical device registered as a class II acute upper airway obstruction device with the United States Food and Drug Administration. Class II acute upper airway obstruction devices are not FDA approved to be sold over the counter. Since these devices are single-use and the legislation does not explicitly cite the number of devices per school, our estimate assumes that each school would be required to stock multiple airway clearance devices. The cost for a case of FDA approved devices is approximately $2,000. To stock all schools with a case of airway clearance devices would result in a $5,468,000 one-time expense in the fiscal year that the legislation takes effect. OMB's estimate of this legislation's impact on the City's expenditures is consistent with the Council's estimate insofar as OMB estimates some cost, however OMB did not provide a specific estimate.

records.title: A Local Law to amend the administrative code of the city of New York and the New York city building code, in relation to cooling systems in tenant-occupied dwellings
agencies_full: Department of Housing Preservation and Development

program_breakdowns.description: Bi-annual A/C filter replacement in units beginning in Fiscal Year 2029.
program_breakdowns.offset_notes: OMB estimate; Council assumes existing resources would be utilized

program_breakdowns.description: Upfront capital cost for cooling systems in NYCHA units.
program_breakdowns.offset_notes: OMB estimate; exact amount uncertain per Council

records.impact_narrative_revenue: It is anticipated that there would be no impact on revenues resulting from the enactment of this legislation. The Office of Management and Budget's (OMB) estimate of this legislation's impact on the City's revenues is consistent with the Council's estimate.
records.impact_narrative_expenditure: It is estimated that there would be no impact on expenditures resulting from the enactment of this legislation, as HPD and the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) would utilize existing resources to fulfill its requirements. OMB's estimate differs from the Council's estimate, where OMB assumes a $282,000 annual expenditure in Other Than Personal Services (OTPS), beginning in Fiscal Year 2029, to replace A/C filters bi-annually in units. records.title: A Local Law to amend the administrative code of the city of New York, in relation to the creation of affordable homeownership opportunities
agencies_full: Department of Housing Preservation and Development

program_breakdowns.description: Additional capital expenditures for HPD to create homeownership opportunity units as required by the legislation.
program_breakdowns.offset_notes: OMB estimates $85 million annually but provides no details; Council estimate is $31.75 million based on current HPD projections and specific homeownership unit requirements.

records.impact_narrative_revenue: It is estimated that there would be no impact on revenues resulting from the enactment of this legislation. The Council's estimate is consistent with the Office of Management and Budget's (OMB) estimate.
records.impact_narrative_expenditure: It is estimated that the enactment of this legislation could result in additional capital expenditures of up to $31,750,000 annually for HPD. This estimate is based on current projections of HPD's affordable homeownership production and the requirement for specific levels of homeownership units as would be required by this legislation. OMB's estimate is not consistent with the Council's. OMB assumes an annual increase in capital spending of $85 million but provides no details on how these totals are determined, so the Council is unable to further assess how the estimates differ. The Council agrees with OMB's assessment that actual costs will be highly dependent on a variety of factors including, but not limited to, housing market conditions, interest rates, capital subsidy levels, and overall HPD capital spending.
records.omb_estimate_notes: OMB provided an estimate of $85 million in annual capital spending increase, but provided no details on how these totals were determined. OMB's estimate is not consistent with the Council's estimate of $31.75 million annually. Both parties agree that actual costs will be dependent on housing market conditions, interest rates, capital subsidy levels, and overall HPD capital spending.
records.estimate_prepared_by: Carla Naranjo, Financial Analyst; Spencer Kuhn, Financial Analyst

records.impact_narrative_revenue: It is anticipated that there would be no impact on revenues resulting from the enactment of this legislation. The Office of Management and Budget's (OMB) estimate of this legislation's impact on the City's revenues is consistent with the Council's estimate.

records.impact_narrative_revenue: This legislation recognizes $3.1 billion in greater than projected City funds revenues in Fiscal 2026. This is primarily driven by increases of $1.6 billion from the personal income and pass-through entity taxes and $310 million from the general sales tax. This was partially offset by a $335 million decrease in the business corporation tax. In addition, miscellaneous revenues increased by $56 million since the last revenue modification, including $30 million in fines and forfeitures and $47 million in miscellaneous revenue. This was partially offset by a $22 million decline in rental income. Unrestricted aid increased by $500 million.
